passage: Dinner was in twenty minutes, and the cricket highlights were on. "Give it!" Farhan grabbed the remote off the arm of the sofa just as Naveen snatched it back. "It's my turn, you had the cartoons!" "No, you did!" They were both standing now, voices rising over the hum of the ceiling fan. Farhan felt his face go hot; he wanted the match, and he wanted to win the argument even more. Then their mother's voice came from the kitchen: "Should I decide, or will you two?" Farhan gulped, took the kitchen timer from the shelf, and set it. "Ten minutes each. You first, since I grabbed." Naveen blinked, then sat down.

qa.q: How long before dinner were the boys fighting over the remote?
How did Farhan feel while grabbing the remote, and what did he want most?
qa.a: He felt angry and competitive, as his hot face shows; he wanted the match, and even more he wanted to win the argument.

qa.q: Which choice worked for the boys, and why?
qa.a: Using the kitchen timer and taking turns worked, because it was fair and stopped the shouting and grabbing.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Farhan offered him the first turn?
qa.a: Surprised and probably a bit relieved, since he blinked and then sat down instead of arguing.

grounding: A child fights over the TV remote with his brother and switches to a timer for fair turns, under time pressure before dinner.

passage:
Wednesday
Big fight with Amit over the remote today. I wanted the cricket highlights, he wanted his cartoon. He grabbed, I grabbed, the back of the remote flew off and the batteries rolled under the sofa. We were both shouting when Mummy walked in. Worst part: my friend Yusuf was visiting and just sat there staring at the floor. So embarrassing.
Mummy didn't shout. She put her phone timer on the table. "Twenty minutes each. Toss for who goes first." Amit won the toss. I sulked for five minutes, but then his cartoon was actually funny, and Yusuf laughed, and I laughed too.
My turn came exactly when the timer rang. No shouting needed. Might ask for the timer every day.
Sumit

qa.q: What happened to the remote during the fight?
qa.a: The back flew off and the batteries rolled under the sofa.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel with Yusuf watching the fight?
qa.a: Embarrassed, especially because Yusuf just sat staring at the floor.

qa.q: Why did the timer work better than grabbing?
qa.a: Each got a fair twenty minutes and a toss decided who went first, so nobody needed to shout.

qa.q: How might Amit have seen the fight?
qa.a: Amit wanted his cartoon just as much and probably felt grabbed from too; the timer gave him a fair turn.

grounding: A child fighting a brother over the TV remote finds that a timer and a parent's decision are fairer than shouting and grabbing.

passage:
In their village near Karnal, the power came back at seven and the TV flickered on. Mohit wanted the wrestling. His younger brother Pranav wanted the animal show. Both lunged for the remote at once.
"I had it first!"
"You always have it first!"
Pranav's elbow knocked the steel glass off the charpai, and water spread across the floor. The shouting brought Baba in from the cattle shed.
Mohit expected a scolding. Instead Baba sat down. "One TV, two boys. What's fair?"
Mohit mumbled, "Half and half?"
"And who goes first?"
Pranav held up a coin. Mohit called heads and lost. He watched the lions with his arms folded, but by the end he was asking questions about the cubs. Then the wrestling came on, and Pranav cheered louder than him.

qa.q: When did the power come back?
What was Mohit feeling when Baba came in?
qa.a: He felt nervous, expecting a scolding.

qa.q: How did Baba help the brothers settle it?
qa.a: He asked them what was fair, so they agreed on half and half and tossed a coin for who went first.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt watching the wrestling?
qa.a: He seemed happy and relieved the fight was over, cheering even louder than Mohit.

grounding: Two brothers fighting over the TV remote settle it fairly by taking turns once a parent helps them decide.
